note: FNS 1044 requires detailed verification of educational grants, scholarships, and loans: source, amount, time period, earmarked amounts for allowable expenses, amounts used for tuition/fees/books/supplies/transportation, and loan origination fees/insurance premiums. The OLG takes a fundamentally different approach — it treats all educational income that is part of a financial aid package, grant, loan, or scholarship as noncountable income and explicitly instructs workers: 'you must not request verification of any type of educational income.' The OLG's Unearned Income Overview page briefly mentions that educational income designated for living expenses must be averaged over the period provided, implying some portion could be countable, but provides no verification procedures for determining which amounts are for living expenses vs. tuition/fees. The OLG does not address verification of income source (Title IV, BIA, etc.), earmarked amounts, allowable expense documentation, or loan origination fees. This appears to be an intentional Massachusetts policy simplification — treating educational income as categorically noncountable rather than requiring the detailed breakdown FNS specifies — but the result is that the OLG provides no guidance for the edge cases where educational income portions designated for living expenses become countable.

_layer3.note: 106 CMR 365.740(B) explicitly requires exclusion of educational income 'to the extent that it is made available for tuition, mandatory school fees, origination fees and insurance premiums on student loans, books, supplies, transportation, and any other expenses necessitated by school attendance.' This mirrors FNS 1044's detailed breakdown. CMR 363.230(D) (referenced but not provided) governs verification of educational loans, grants, and scholarships. The state regulation mandates the same verification distinction FNS requires: determining which portions are for allowable expenses (excludable) vs. living expenses (countable). The OLG's blanket exclusion of all educational income without verification contradicts the regulatory requirement to verify which amounts are earmarked for specific expense categories.
